transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Gomez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Head of ML - DataBridge), Priya Nair (SRE), Liam O'Connor (Eng Manager)
---
[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Alicia from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, Samir my SE is with me. Mike, Priya, Liam, thanks for making time.
[00:10] Michael: Yeah, thanks. We wanted to dig into the benchmark plan and how to integrate our scripts with your harness. We have a pretty typical production workload but some streaming use-cases too.
[00:22] Samir: Cool. Quick agenda: nail success criteria, get sizing (RPS / tokens per request), discuss harness integration (how your scripts plug in), and streaming vs non-streaming behavior differences. Also logistics for running a full load on Dedicated vs hosted.
[00:34] Liam: Sounds good. For context, our primary success criteria are P95 latency under 250ms for short queries (~150 tokens), and sustained throughput of about 120 requests per second for the classification route. Quality threshold: identical or better vs our current OpenAI baseline on the classification F1.
[00:50] Michael: And we have another path for longer generative prompts where we do streaming to the client, target P50 latency under 500ms for first token and reasonable tail.
[01:05] Priya: Security side: we'll need SOC2 docs, KMS integration, and VPC peering if we run a Dedicated instance. Also audit logs retention.
[01:18] Alicia: Noted. We'll share the SOC2 and VPC checklist. Samir, on the P95 250ms, are you expecting that on hosted or Dedicated?
[01:26] Samir: There's a tradeoff. Hosted can be great for quick tests but Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency because you control the GPU pool. For 120 RPS sustained, Dedicated is the safer bet. But we can run an initial benchmark on hosted to validate correctness and then move to Dedicated for the loaded run.
[01:42] Michael: Ok, we were hoping to avoid upfront Dedicated until we prove perf, but we can do an initial proof on hosted. What do you need from our side to run the harness?
[01:53] Samir: Two main things: your canonical workload scripts (preferably in Python/Node) that call your existing wrapper, and a sample of payload distributions — request size histogram, concurrency pattern, and a short trace of real requests. Ideally a small repre dataset for quality evals.
[02:08] Michael: We can share a 24-48 hour trace and a couple of production scripts. They include both streaming and non-streaming endpoints. Any specifics on how to instrument streaming?
[02:18] Samir: Yes. Our harness supports streaming via a websocket or SSE shim. For streaming tests we'll need to capture client consumption pattern (how often clients read partials), average tokens sent per second, and expected end-to-end latency target for first byte vs completion. If you can't share the client, a simulated consumer that reads at the observed cadence is sufficient.
[02:36] Priya: Side note, our streaming is sensitive to head-of-line blocking. If the runtime does batching for throughput, can that cause larger first-token latency for streaming?
[02:46] Samir: Good callout. The balance between batching and latency is exactly the tradeoff. Our runtime does continuous batching and also supports low-latency fast-paths for streaming where we prioritize P0 tokens. We'll surface knob settings in the harness so you can tune batching windows and max batch size.
[03:02] Liam: Can you quantify how much batching impacts first-token latency? Ballpark numbers?
[03:07] Samir: Roughly, if you let batch windows grow for throughput, P50 first-token could increase from ~60ms to ~150-250ms depending on request rate and model. Dedicated with reserved GPUs and smaller batch windows can keep first-token in the sub-150ms range. But exacts depend on model size and quantization.
[03:24] Michael: We're also planning to test a quantized 4-bit variant. Does your harness support comparing different quantization profiles?
[03:30] Samir: Yes, the harness can run parallel variants and collect latency/throughput/quality tradeoffs. We'll need model artifacts or model name if using public models; for private ones we'll need the saved quantized model or Redwood can help onboard a model to a private repo.
[03:44] Alicia: Quick question on metrics: which metrics will we report back? We usually send P50, P95, P99 latencies, accuracy/F1 for classification, avg tokens per request, token throughput (tokens/sec) and cost estimates. Anything else you'd want?
[03:58] Michael: Can you add jitter and error-rate breakdowns too? And a tps by time-of-day graph so we can spot spikes.
[04:05] Samir: Yep. We'll include error codes, timeouts, and a scatter of latency vs payload size. Also KV cache hit-rate if you enable prefix caching.
[04:14] Priya: You said "KV cash" earlier — I think you mean KV cache, right?
[04:18] Samir: Sorry, yes, KV cache. Sometimes the transcript likes to mangle that.
[04:22] Liam: For harness integration, what's the expected format for the scripts? We have a fairly opinionated SDK and wrapper.
[04:29] Samir: We support a few adapter hooks: 1) http shim where you point harness at an endpoint (auth token provided), 2) local script runner where harness calls your script that implements a small interface (send payload, receive response), or 3) a replay mode that replays a captured trace. The simplest for initial tests is replay mode + a thin shim to map your request/response shapes.
[04:49] Michael: Replay sounds easiest. We'll sanitize traces and give you a sample load file. Any limits on trace size?
[04:55] Samir: No strict limit but for practicality keep initial uploads to a few GBs. For the full load run you can give us the long trace on S3.
[05:04] Alicia: On timelines: if you can share traces and scripts by next Tuesday (2026-04-06), we can run a hosted sanity test by mid-next-week and schedule a Dedicated full-load run the week after that. Does that work?
[05:16] Michael: Yes that timeline works. We'll aim for 2026-04-06 for artifacts.
[05:20] Priya: About VPC / private deploy: if we move to Dedicated, we'll want customer-managed VPC and KMS. How long does setup take?
[05:28] Samir: Provisioning customer-vpc Dedicated typically takes 2-5 business days once networking is finalized. KMS onboarding depends on your provider—if it's AWS KMS and we have keys pre-shared it's quick, otherwise a week. We'll send a checklist.
[05:41] Liam: What about cost estimation during the POC? We need a rough monthly estimate for the Dedicated config to get budget approval.
[05:49] Alicia: We'll provide a ballpark based on the throughput target — Samir will prepare a config + cost estimate as an action item. It won't be final but enough for budgeting.
[05:58] Michael: On quality checks: we'll run the same evals against your outputs vs our OpenAI baseline. How do you collect output for quality scoring?
[06:06] Samir: The harness can capture outputs for each replayed request and run your evaluation script (you can provide a scorer) or we can run a standard F1/precision/recall. For generative prompts we can do prompt-level BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific metrics.
[06:21] Priya: Are there concerns about data retention from these traces? We need to ensure retention policies and that logs aren't kept beyond the POC without consent.
[06:29] Alicia: We'll honor retention policies; we'll document retention and deletion steps and can sign DPA language if needed.
[06:36] Michael: One more technical: streaming vs non-streaming—if we do streaming in the harness, do you simulate network delays? We have mobile clients that are lossy.
[06:44] Samir: Yes, the harness can simulate client-side consumption patterns and network delay. That helps uncover head-of-line blocking or chunking behavior.
[06:52] Liam: For the full-load run, do you recommend any particular model variants or quantization settings upfront?
[06:58] Samir: Start with your production model footprint; run 8-bit (or 4-bit if you want lower memory) variants in parallel. The harness can compare them side-by-side. If you expect strict latency, lean toward less aggressive quantization on the hot path.
[07:12] Michael: How do we interpret cost numbers — token-level cost vs infra amortized cost?
[07:17] Samir: We'll provide both: per-token inference cost and total infra cost for the Dedicated config (GPU hours + expected utilization). Also an estimate of cost delta if you move from hosted to Dedicated.
[07:28] Priya: Any red flags we've missed? Things that commonly break POCs?
[07:33] Samir: Two common ones: 1) mismatch between replay payload shape and actual live requests (so ensure sanitization preserves shape), 2) underestimating client-side consumption patterns for streaming which affects latency.
[07:44] Alicia: Ok let's recap action items and owners.
[07:48] Michael: Quick Q: can we run a dry run ourselves before handing artifacts? Like run your harness locally?
[07:53] Samir: Yes, the harness is open-source and can be run locally — we'll share a quickstart. That helps find mapping issues early.
[08:02] Alicia: Recap: Redwood to share harness repo and SOC2 + VPC checklist. DataBridge to share trace, scripts, sample payloads by 2026-04-06. Samir to prepare Dedicated config + cost estimate by 2026-04-07. Priya to provide security questions. We'll schedule hosted sanity test mid-next-week and Dedicated full-load the following week.
[08:20] Michael: That matches our expectations. Appreciate the clarity.
[08:24] Priya: Thanks all, we'll get the artifacts ready.
[08:27] Liam: Thanks.
[08:30] Alicia: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and links after the call.
[08:33] (end)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hearings (KV cash -> KV cache), some speaker label simplifications, and pauses.
notes: Participants agreed on artifacts and timeline for hosted sanity test then Dedicated full-load. Redwood to share harness + security docs. Customer to supply traces and scripts. SE to provide Dedicated config + cost.
